title: Lennon's Kid Mode: How It Works

items.title: What's on This Page
items.why:
How Lennon's kid mode would work, from your earlier picks: teach push-ups, sit-ups and good form; stars for good-form moves; stars become Dragon Balls; all seven earn a wish, a real prize a grown-up sets behind a code.

This page is only about how it works. Pictures of the screens come on the next page, after your picks. Nothing is built.

Amounts and safety come from the sources named on each card. Which moves, and the game rules, are my judgement.

items.title: The Four Moves
items.why:
1. Push-up: starts against a wall, then on the knees, then a full push-up.
2. Curl-up: knees bent, feet flat and not held, lift the shoulders a little and slide the hands forward. Used instead of a full sit-up.
3. Squat: no weight.
4. Plank: starts on the knees, then on the toes.

KidsHealth: kids can start with body-weight moves such as sit-ups, push-ups and squats.
FitnessGram manual: the curl-up is "both safer and more effective" than a sit-up, because it doesn't use the hip flexors.
CDC: push-ups count as muscle-strengthening for children.

options.label: These four plus jumping
options.desc: Star jumps. CDC counts jumping as bone-strengthening for children, at least 3 days a week.

options.label: Needs changes
options.desc: Type them in the notes.

items.title: Sliders and Medicine Balls
items.why:
You picked sliders and the two mini medicine balls as Lennon's equipment.

I found no health source on sliders for children, and none that says what medicine ball weight suits a 7-year-old. Nationwide Children's lists medicine balls as fine for kids' strength training, without a weight.

The Danskin ball is 5 lb; the Gaiam ball's weight is unknown.

options.label: Body weight only for now
options.desc: The sliders and balls stay in his equipment list but aren't used in kid mode.

options.label: Add one ball move
options.desc: A gentle chest pass to a grown-up. You pick which ball.

items.title: How Long, How Often
items.why:
KidsHealth: start with one or two sets of 8 to 12, at least 20 to 30 minutes, 2 or 3 days a week, with a day off between, after a 5 to 10 minute warm-up.
AAP: attention spans of 6 to 9 year olds are still short; teach in short pieces.
CDC: muscle-strengthening at least 3 days a week, as part of 60 minutes of activity every day (play counts).

No source gives a shorter session for a child who is easily distracted.

options.label: 3 days, 1 round, about 10 minutes
options.desc: Each move once, 8 reps (plank: up to 20 seconds). A second round is offered once that's easy. Shorter than KidsHealth's 20 to 30 minutes; the rest of his activity is play.

options.label: 3 days, 2 rounds, about 20 minutes
options.desc: Matches KidsHealth from the start, with the warm-up.

items.title: How a Star Is Earned
items.why: The app can't see his form. KidsHealth and AAP both say kids' strength work should be closely supervised, so a grown-up is there anyway.

options.label: A grown-up taps the star
options.desc: After each move: "Good form?" Yes gives a star. No shows the tip again and he can try once more.

options.label: Lennon taps it himself
options.desc: A star for every finished move. Simpler, but stars don't depend on form.

items.title: Stars to Dragon Balls
items.why:
With 4 moves, a full workout gives 4 stars.

At 3 workouts a week:

options.label: 4 stars = 1 Dragon Ball
options.desc: One ball per good workout. A wish about every 2 to 3 weeks.

options.label: 8 stars = 1 Dragon Ball
options.desc: A wish about every 5 weeks.

options.label: 12 stars = 1 Dragon Ball
options.desc: A wish about every 7 weeks.

items.title: The Wish
items.why: A grown-up sets the prize ahead of time, behind a code, so it's a surprise until all seven are gathered. AAP says food should not be used as a reward, and suggests stickers and praise instead.

options.label: A grown-up types the prize
options.desc: Anything, such as "Trip to the park". The setup screen notes "not food".

options.label: Pick from a list
options.desc: Extra screen time, a trip, a small toy... a grown-up can also type one.

items.title: After a Wish
items.why: Today the Dragon Balls and the wish happen only once.

options.label: The balls scatter and he collects again
options.desc: A grown-up sets the next prize.

items.title: The Grown-Up Code
items.why: The prize, the settings and switching to another person sit behind the code.

options.label: A 4-digit code
options.desc: Set when kid mode starts. Separate from the app's own lock.

options.label: Use the app's own lock
options.desc: The same PIN that opens the app.

items.title: What Lennon Sees
items.why: The full app has food logs, weight, calendars and charts.

options.label: Only kid mode
options.desc: The workout, his stars and his Dragon Balls. Everything else behind the grown-up code.

options.label: Kid mode plus the rest
options.desc: Kid mode on Home, the other tabs as now.

items.title: Form Tips
items.why:
One short tip per move, in kid words. I found no form tips written for children, so these are simplified from Cleveland Clinic, NHS and FitnessGram:

Push-up: "Body straight like a board."
Curl-up: "Slide your hands, then lie back down."
Squat: "Knees point at your toes. Chest up."
Plank: "Straight like a board. Don't let your bottom sag."

options.label: Tip on screen, and read aloud
options.desc: Uses the tablet's own voice; no internet needed.

options.label: Needs changes
options.desc: Type them in the notes.

items.title: Safety Line
items.why:
AAP: "Stop lifting at once if pain is felt." KidsHealth: most injuries happen when a child is goofing around and not supervised.

The weighted vest and ankle weights stay out of kid mode; I found no source on them for children.

options.label: One line on the workout screen
options.desc: "Grown-up nearby. If anything hurts, stop and tell them."
